caesar: Walter Chell, restaurant manager at the Calgary Inn, created the Caesar in 1969 to mark the opening of the hotel's Italian restaurant, Marco's. He drew on spaghetti alle vongole, the clam and tomato pasta he recalled from Venice, and mixed mashed clams into a tomato base seasoned with Worcestershire sauce and celery salt. His granddaughter has said his Italian roots gave it the name, and the story goes that an English regular's praise for his bloody Caesar is why many Canadians still call it a Bloody Caesar.
greyhound: The Greyhound takes its name from the Post House restaurants that the Greyhound bus company ran in its terminals, where a 1945 article in Harper's Magazine described it as gin, sugar and canned grapefruit juice. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book had printed a similar gin and grapefruit drink in 1930, but not under that name. After the Second World War vodka gradually took gin's place, and a salted rim turned the same drink into its sibling, the Salty Dog.
brandy-alexander: The Alexander began as a gin drink: Hugo Ensslin's 1916 Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York, includes one of gin, crème de cacao and cream. Who it honors is disputed; one account credits Troy Alexander, a bartender at Rector's in New York, who made a white drink for a dinner celebrating Phoebe Snow, a railroad's advertising character, and another ties the brandy version to the 1922 London wedding of Princess Mary. Brandy eventually displaced gin, and John Lennon, introduced to it by Harry Nilsson in the 1970s, reportedly said it tasted like a milkshake.
espresso-martini: Dick Bradsell created the drink in London around 1983 at the Soho Brasserie, where, he said, the coffee machine stood right next to his station. The usual story is that a customer, often said to be a well-known model, asked him for something to wake her up, and he shook vodka with fresh espresso, coffee liqueur and sugar, calling it the Vodka Espresso. He later served a version as the Pharmaceutical Stimulant at the Pharmacy in Notting Hill, and the Espresso Martini name took hold in the 1990s, when nearly everything was served in a martini glass.
grasshopper: Tujague's, the old French Quarter restaurant in New Orleans, credits Philibert Guichet, one of its owners, with the Grasshopper, usually dated to 1918, and says he created it for a cocktail competition in New York and took second place, though historians have found no record of the contest. The name comes from the bright green of the crème de menthe. The drink found its widest audience decades later as a sweet after-dinner order, and Tujague's still serves it.
porto-flip: Flips began as a colonial American tavern drink of beer, rum and sugar, frothed by plunging a red-hot iron called a loggerhead into the mug. Over the 19th century the beer dropped out, eggs went in and the drink was served cold, and Jerry Thomas's 1887 bar guide includes a port wine flip among its many versions. The Porto Flip, port with brandy and egg yolk, is the family's best-known survivor and sits on the International Bartenders Association's list of classic cocktails.
white-russian: The White Russian first turns up in print in the Oakland Tribune in November 1965, as equal parts vodka, cream and Coffee Southern, a coffee liqueur made by the Southern Comfort company. It is the Black Russian with cream added; that drink is credited to Gustave Tops, who mixed vodka and coffee liqueur at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels in 1949, and the Russian in both names refers only to the vodka. The White Russian drifted out of fashion until the 1998 film The Big Lebowski made it the signature of its bathrobe-wearing hero, the Dude.
gin-fizz: The fizz first appears in print in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide: a sour of spirit, citrus and sugar, shaken and topped with soda water, named for its effervescence. Gin soon became the favorite base, and around the turn of the 20th century the gin fizz was an American institution. New Orleans bartenders built on it, most famously Henry Ramos, and a family of variations followed, from the silver fizz with egg white to the golden fizz with the yolk.
ramos-gin-fizz: Henry C. Ramos created his fizz in 1888 at the Imperial Cabinet Saloon in New Orleans, calling it the New Orleans Fizz. Cream, egg white and orange flower water needed long shaking, so at his later bar, the Stag, he kept a line of shaker boys passing each drink along, reportedly around 35 of them during the 1915 Mardi Gras. After Prohibition the Roosevelt Hotel took up the name, and Huey Long famously brought one of its bartenders to New York to show reporters how the drink was made.
bushwacker: The Bushwacker was first made in 1975 at the Ship's Store and Sapphire Pub in Sapphire Village on St. Thomas, in the US Virgin Islands, and the story goes that it was named after an Afghan hound called Bushwack that belonged to two regulars. Linda Taylor, who managed the bar at the Sandshaker Lounge on Pensacola Beach, tasted it on a trip to St. Thomas in 1977 and reworked it back home with rum in place of vodka and a swirl of chocolate syrup. Pensacola Beach has held an annual Bushwacker festival since 1986.
frozen-margarita: Dallas restaurateur Mariano Martinez created the frozen margarita machine in 1971, shortly after opening his restaurant, because his bartenders struggled to blend margaritas consistently. After seeing a Slurpee machine at a 7-Eleven, he converted a secondhand soft-serve ice cream machine to make them, and the idea spread to Tex-Mex restaurants across the country. The original machine was acquired by the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in 2005.
miami-vice: The Miami Vice, a strawberry daiquiri and a piña colada poured side by side in one glass, has no documented inventor, and its name most likely comes from the television crime series set in Miami.
americano: The Americano grew out of the Milano-Torino, served at Gaspare Campari's café in Milan from the 1860s: bitter Campari from Milan with sweet vermouth from Turin. A splash of soda water lengthened it, and the usual explanation for the new name is that American visitors took to the drink, though nobody has pinned down when or why it stuck. Swap the soda for gin and you have the Negroni, and Ian Fleming made the Americano the first drink James Bond orders in Casino Royale, published in 1953.
bloody-mary: Fernand Petiot said he first mixed vodka and tomato juice at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the early 1920s. In 1934 he moved to the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis in New York, where he added salt, pepper, lemon and Worcestershire sauce, and the hotel, finding the name indelicate, listed it as the Red Snapper. The entertainer George Jessel also claimed the drink, and a 1939 newspaper column credited him with it. The name has been tied to Queen Mary I of England, to the actress Mary Pickford and to a Chicago bar, but none of these explanations is proven.
cape-codder: Ocean Spray, the cranberry growers' cooperative, published the recipe in 1945 to sell more cranberry juice, calling its mix of vodka, cranberry and lime the Red Devil. The drink was renamed for Cape Cod, the Massachusetts cranberry country, in the early 1960s, and a 1965 mention in The New Yorker called the Cape Codder America's newest cocktail creation. Ocean Spray's campaign to sell cranberry as a mixer went on to shape later drinks such as the Sea Breeze.
cuba-libre: The Cuba Libre takes its name from the rallying cry of Cuba's independence struggle, and it dates to around 1900, when bottled Coca-Cola reached Havana in the wake of the Spanish-American War and the American troops who stayed on. The most famous account comes from Fausto Rodríguez, who in 1965, while working for Bacardi, swore that he had watched a US Army Signal Corps officer order rum and Coca-Cola with lime in a Havana bar in August 1900, prompting a toast to a free Cuba. The calypso Rum and Coca-Cola, a wartime hit for the Andrews Sisters, carried it around the world.
dark-n-stormy: Gosling Brothers, Bermuda's best-known rum family, says the Dark 'n' Stormy was born just after the First World War, when Royal Navy sailors on the island mixed the family's dark rum with ginger beer. The story goes that one sailor compared its color to a storm cloud that only a fool or a dead man would sail under. The classic pairing was Gosling's Black Seal and Barritt's Ginger Beer, and Gosling's holds the name as a trademark in the United States, so a drink sold under it there must be made with Black Seal.
el-diablo: El Diablo first appears in print in Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink in 1946, where Victor Bergeron listed it as the Mexican El Diablo: tequila and crème de cassis with lime, lengthened with ginger. Bergeron ran his Polynesian-themed restaurant in Oakland, California, and tequila was still a novelty in American bars, which makes this one of the earliest tequila cocktails on record. The name is simply Spanish for the devil.
fernet-con-coca: Fernet, the bitter Italian herbal liqueur, reached Argentina with Italian immigrants of the late 19th and early 20th centuries and was long taken after dinner or with soda water. When it was first mixed with cola is unclear: some trace the pairing to the 1950s, while others credit Oscar 'el Negro' Becerra, a drummer and bartender from Cruz del Eje, in the 1970s. University students in Córdoba took it up in the 1980s, Fratelli Branca promoted it nationally, and in 2020 the International Bartenders Association added it to its official list as the Fernandito.
gin-and-tonic: The gin and tonic was born among British officers and officials in 19th-century India, where quinine was taken against malaria. Quinine water was bitter, so they made their ration more palatable with gin, sugar and lime, and commercial tonic water, which appeared in the middle of the century, made the habit easier still; Schweppes later sold an Indian Tonic Water. The pairing came home with returning officers and became a fixture of British life.
gin-rickey: The rickey was born in the 1880s at Shoomaker's, a Washington, D.C. bar on the strip known as Rum Row, and is named for Colonel Joe Rickey, a Democratic lobbyist who took his bourbon with lime and sparkling mineral water and no sugar. Bartender George Williamson is credited with making it a house drink, and by the 1890s the gin version had overtaken the original, which became known as the Joe Rickey. In 2011 the D.C. Council declared the rickey Washington's native cocktail, and local bartenders now mark July as Rickey Month.
long-island-iced-tea: Robert 'Rosebud' Butt says he created the Long Island Iced Tea in 1972 at the Oak Beach Inn on Long Island, New York, as his entry in a contest to invent a new drink using triple sec. He combined several white spirits with sour mix and a splash of cola, which gave the drink the look of iced tea although it contains none. A competing story places an earlier version on Long Island, an island in the Holston River at Kingsport, Tennessee, during Prohibition, credited to a man known as Old Man Bishop and later altered by his son Ransom.
mojito: Cuban lore traces the Mojito to El Draque, a rough mix of aguardiente, lime, sugar and mint said to be named after the English privateer Francis Drake, though that link is legend rather than record. The documented trail is later: a recipe called Mojo Criollo appeared in a Cuban drinks book in 1927, and the Mojito, under that name, was on the souvenir menu of Havana's Sloppy Joe's Bar for the 1931 season. The name may come from mojo, a Cuban lime-based seasoning, or from mojadito, little wet one, and its ties to Hemingway and La Bodeguita del Medio are popular but unproven.
moscow-mule: The Moscow Mule is usually dated to 1941 and the Cock 'n' Bull, a British-style pub on the Sunset Strip in Los Angeles. Owner Jack Morgan was struggling to sell his ginger beer, and John G. Martin of Heublein had bought the rights to Smirnoff, a vodka few Americans then drank; together they turned the two into one drink. The pub's head bartender, Wes Price, later said he mixed the first one himself to clear dead stock. Martin then toured bars with a Polaroid camera, photographing bartenders holding a copper mug and a bottle of Smirnoff, and the drink spread nationwide.
paloma: The Paloma, a highball of tequila, lime and grapefruit soda, has no documented inventor or date, though it is widely regarded as the most popular tequila cocktail in Mexico itself.
pimms-cup: By the usual account Pimm's dates to the 1840s, though some histories say 1823, when James Pimm, a farmer's son from Kent who ran an oyster bar in the City of London, served a gin-based digestive of herbs and liqueurs in small tankards known as the No. 1 Cup. Demand from other bars led to large-scale production in 1851. Topped up with lemonade and garnished with fruit, the long summer cup became a drink of English garden parties, and Wimbledon has had a Pimm's bar since 1971.
ranch-water: Ranch Water has no recorded inventor; Texas lore places it on West Texas ranches, where, the story goes, ranchers drank an inch from a bottle of Topo Chico, the sparkling mineral water from Monterrey, Mexico, and topped it up with tequila and lime. Austin restaurateur Kevin Williamson, who says he first drank something similar while hunting with his father, helped make it a menu fixture at his restaurant Ranch 616, and the historic Gage Hotel in Marathon serves it too.
screwdriver: In 1949 Time magazine described the latest Yankee concoction of vodka and orange juice, called a screwdriver, being drunk in an Istanbul hotel bar where American engineers mingled with Turkish intelligence agents and Balkan refugees. The usual story is that oil workers or engineers abroad, lacking a spoon, stirred the mix with a screwdriver, though nobody has confirmed it. The drink rose with vodka itself in the United States through the 1950s.
sea-breeze: A cocktail called the Sea Breeze existed by the late 1920s, but it was a gin drink with grenadine, and 1930s versions added apricot brandy and lemon juice. The version made today, vodka with cranberry and grapefruit juice, descends from Ocean Spray's campaign to sell cranberry juice as a mixer, which began with the Red Devil, later the Cape Codder, and it did not become widely popular until the 1970s.
seven-and-seven: The Seven and Seven is named for its two brands: Seagram's 7 Crown, a blended American whiskey introduced after the end of Prohibition, and 7 Up, the lemon-lime soda. No bartender has claimed the pairing, but it had become one of America's most popular bar orders by the disco era, and in Saturday Night Fever John Travolta's Tony Manero orders one.
tequila-sunrise: The Tequila Sunrise most bars make today, tequila and orange juice with grenadine, was created in the early 1970s by bartenders Bobby Lozoff and Billy Rice at the Trident in Sausalito, California. Mick Jagger tried one at a party at the bar before the Rolling Stones' 1972 tour, the band's touring party took it up across America, and Jose Cuervo later printed the recipe on its bottles. An older drink of the same name, tequila with crème de cassis and lime, had been served at the Arizona Biltmore hotel in the 1930s.
tinto-de-verano: Tinto de Verano is usually traced to Córdoba in Andalusia, where, early in the 20th century, Federico Vargas mixed red wine with soda for customers at his roadside inn, the Venta de Vargas, who at first simply asked for un Vargas. As the drink travelled across Spain it took the name tinto de verano, summer red wine, and lemon soda became a common partner. Many Spaniards order it in preference to sangria, which they tend to think of as a drink for visitors.
tom-collins: The Tom Collins was established in American bars by the 1870s, but its roots run back to London, where a gin punch was credited to John Collins, headwaiter at Limmer's Old House in Mayfair. Two explanations compete for the switch from John to Tom: bartenders' use of sweetened Old Tom gin, and the Great Tom Collins Hoax of 1874, when Americans told friends that a man called Tom Collins was insulting them in a nearby bar, sending them off to find a man who did not exist.
whiskey-highball: Patrick Gavin Duffy, who ran a bar in New York, claimed he introduced the highball to America in the mid-1890s, serving Scotch with ice and soda water as British drinkers already did, though Boston's Adams House made a rival claim. The name may come from ball, an old word for a glass, or from railroad signals, and neither theory is settled. Japan took up the highball after the Second World War, a 2008 Suntory campaign revived it there, and specialist highball bars followed.
hot-toddy: The word toddy came into English from India, where it named a drink of fermented palm sap, and by 1786 it was used in Britain for spirits mixed with hot water, sugar and spices. Scotland has long claimed the hot whisky version, sweetened with honey or sugar and sharpened with lemon, as its own. One Edinburgh tale links the name to Tod's Well, a spring that once supplied the city's water, though the Indian root is far better attested.
irish-coffee: Joe Sheridan, head chef at the flying boat terminal at Foynes on the Shannon estuary, created Irish coffee around 1943; the usual story is that he added whiskey to the coffee of passengers whose flight had turned back on a cold night, and when asked whether it was Brazilian coffee, said it was Irish coffee. In 1952 the San Francisco travel writer Stanton Delaplane brought the idea to the Buena Vista Cafe, where he and owner Jack Koeppler worked out how to make the cream float, and Sheridan later moved to San Francisco to work there.
mint-julep: Juleps were sweetened medicinal drinks in Europe long before Americans added mint and spirits; the word traces through Arabic to the Persian gulab, rosewater. In 1803 the English traveller John Davis described the mint julep as a dram of spirit with mint steeped in it, taken by Virginians in the morning, and Senator Henry Clay of Kentucky is said to have introduced it to Washington at the Willard Hotel's Round Robin Bar. Bourbon became its spirit of choice, and since 1938 it has been the signature drink of the Kentucky Derby.
sherry-cobbler: The earliest known mention of the Sherry Cobbler comes from 1838, in the diary of the traveller Katherine Jane Ellice, and within a few years it was among the most fashionable mixed drinks in America: sherry, sugar and orange shaken over plenty of ice. Its rise rode on a growing trade in ice and on the drinking straw, and Charles Dickens gave it international fame in Martin Chuzzlewit, where a character marvels at sipping one through a straw. The origin of the name is unclear, and the drink faded after Prohibition.
bentons-old-fashioned: Don Lee created Benton's Old Fashioned in 2007 at PDT, the New York speakeasy-style bar in the East Village entered through a phone booth in a hot dog shop. He infused bourbon with rendered bacon fat from Benton's Smoky Mountain Country Hams, Allan Benton's smokehouse in Madisonville, Tennessee, then chilled it and lifted off the solid fat, a technique called fat-washing that Eben Freeman had pioneered at WD-50. Finished in the old fashioned style, it became PDT's signature and is widely credited with bringing fat-washing into bars everywhere.
bramble: Dick Bradsell created the Bramble in 1984 at Fred's Club in Soho, London. Wanting a distinctly British drink, he drew on childhood memories of picking blackberries on the Isle of Wight, building a gin sour over crushed ice and drizzling crème de mûre, a blackberry liqueur, over the top. The name is the country word for the blackberry bush, and the drink became one of the defining classics of London's cocktail revival.
breakfast-martini: Salvatore Calabrese created the Breakfast Martini in 1996 at the Library Bar of the Lanesborough hotel in London. He has said the idea came at the breakfast table, when his wife insisted he eat before work and the bitter orange marmalade on his toast stayed with him, so he shook a spoonful of marmalade with gin, Cointreau and lemon juice. The drink descends from the White Lady and other gin and orange liqueur sours, and it spread from London to menus abroad.
chartreuse-swizzle: Marcovaldo Dionysos created the Chartreuse Swizzle in San Francisco in the early 2000s for a cocktail competition run by the makers of Chartreuse, swizzling green Chartreuse with pineapple juice, lime and falernum over crushed ice and borrowing a Caribbean format for an alpine liqueur. Chartreuse itself comes from the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse monastery in the mountains near Grenoble, whose recipe of around 130 plants is known only to a few members of the order. The swizzle has since become a modern classic on tiki and craft menus alike.
division-bell: Phil Ward created the Division Bell in 2009 at Mayahuel, the New York bar he opened that year to celebrate tequila and mezcal, named for the Aztec goddess of the agave plant. He paired the smoke of mezcal with Aperol, maraschino and lime, and named the drink after Pink Floyd's album The Division Bell, which takes its own title from the bell that calls members of the British Parliament to vote. It was one of a wave of drinks from Ward and his colleagues that brought mezcal from specialty shelves into mainstream cocktail bars.
eastside: George Delgado is usually credited with the Eastside, created in 2004 at Libation, a bar on New York's Lower East Side, as a long drink of gin, lime, sugar, cucumber and mint. Bartender Christy Pope took it to Sasha Petraske's Milk & Honey, where the version served up, without soda, took shape. The drink updates the Southside, the minted gin sour of the Prohibition era, and its name plays on its parent's.
final-ward: Phil Ward created the Final Ward in New York around 2007; it is usually credited to Death & Co, though Ward has said he first made it at the Pegu Club, where he tended bar beforehand. It reworks the Last Word, an equal-parts drink from the Detroit Athletic Club that Seattle bartender Murray Stenson brought back into circulation, swapping gin for rye and lime for lemon while keeping green Chartreuse and maraschino. The name is a double pun: his final word on the Last Word, with his own surname worked in.
french-martini: The French Martini comes from the New York restaurants of British-born restaurateur Keith McNally. Accounts date it to the late 1980s, part of the wave of vodka drinks served in martini glasses, and it reached a wide audience in the late 1990s on the menus of his bar Pravda and his restaurant Balthazar, becoming a staple of the decade's 'tini craze. The only French ingredient is Chambord, a black raspberry liqueur from the Loire Valley, which joins vodka and pineapple juice.
garibaldi: The Garibaldi has no recorded inventor, but its name honors Giuseppe Garibaldi, the general who led the campaign to unify Italy, the usual explanation being that it joins Campari from the north with the oranges of the south; Italians have long ordered it simply as a Campari Orange. Its modern reputation owes much to bartender Naren Young, who at Dante in New York ran the oranges through a high-speed juicer to aerate the juice into what he called fluffy orange juice.
gin-basil-smash: Jörg Meyer created the Gin Basil Smash in 2008 at Le Lion, his bar near Hamburg's city hall. Inspired by the whiskey smash, he muddled basil with lemon juice and sugar syrup, shook it with gin, and at first called the result the Gin Pesto. Renamed, it spread quickly through cocktail blogs and bar menus, first across Germany and then abroad, becoming one of the best-known modern classics from continental Europe.
gin-gin-mule: Audrey Saunders created the Gin-Gin Mule in 2000 at Beacon Restaurant in New York, at a time when vodka dominated American bars and gin was a hard sell. She crossed two familiar favorites, the Moscow Mule and the Mojito, combining gin with fresh mint, lime and a house-made ginger beer, so that vodka drinkers would meet gin on familiar ground. When she opened the Pegu Club in 2005 it became one of the bar's signatures, and it is widely counted among the most influential cocktails of the early 21st century.
gold-rush: The Gold Rush came about around 2000 at Milk & Honey, Sasha Petraske's influential New York bar, when T.J. Siegal, a friend of Petraske's, hit on using honey syrup in place of sugar in a bourbon whiskey sour with fresh lemon. The swap was small but the result caught on, and the Gold Rush became one of the house standards that Milk & Honey's bartenders carried to bars around the world. Sam Ross's Penicillin, created at the same bar, is a smoky Scotch riff on it.
kentucky-buck: Erick Castro created the Kentucky Buck in San Francisco around 2009, and it is associated with Bourbon & Branch and Rickhouse, whiskey bars he worked with in the city. He started from the buck, the old family of highballs built from a spirit, citrus and ginger, and gave it bourbon, lemon, a dash of Angostura bitters and a muddled strawberry for fruit and color. It has since been widely reprinted in cocktail books and on bar menus well beyond San Francisco.
naked-and-famous: Joaquín Simó created the Naked and Famous in 2011 at Death & Co in New York, borrowing the equal-parts structure of the Last Word and the bittersweet balance of Sam Ross's Paper Plane; he has described it as the offspring of the two, born in the mountains of Oaxaca. Smoky mezcal and yellow Chartreuse set it apart from both parents. The name comes from a line in Tricky Kid, a song by the British musician Tricky, and the International Bartenders Association added it to its official list in 2020.
oaxaca-old-fashioned: Phil Ward created the Oaxaca Old Fashioned in 2007 at Death & Co in New York, applying the old fashioned template to agave: reposado tequila with a smaller measure of mezcal, agave nectar and mole bitters. At the time mezcal was barely known in American bars, and the drink is widely credited with introducing many drinkers to it and helping start the mezcal boom of the following years. Ward went on to open Mayahuel, a bar devoted to tequila and mezcal, in 2009, and the drink has become a modern standard on menus far beyond New York.
old-cuban: Audrey Saunders created the Old Cuban in 2001, and it made its debut at Bemelmans Bar in the Carlyle hotel in New York, where she was running the cocktail program. She wanted an elegant Champagne drink with a tropical edge and described the result as a Mojito in a little black dress: aged rum, mint, lime, sugar and Angostura, topped with Champagne. It became a downtown standard after she opened the Pegu Club in 2005.
porn-star-martini: Douglas Ankrah, the London bartender who co-founded the LAB bar in Soho, created the drink in 2002, conceiving it in Cape Town while preparing to open Townhouse, a bar in Knightsbridge, and first calling it the Maverick Martini after a club in that city. Back in London he gave it the provocative name it is known by, saying it simply looked like something a porn star would drink. Built on vanilla vodka and passion fruit, it has repeatedly been ranked the United Kingdom's most popular cocktail.
red-hook: Vincenzo Errico created the Red Hook in 2003 at Milk & Honey in New York, as a riff on the Brooklyn cocktail. He kept rye and maraschino liqueur but used Punt e Mes, a bitter Italian vermouth from Turin, and named the result after Red Hook, the Brooklyn waterfront neighborhood. Its success started a run of drinks named for Brooklyn neighborhoods by New York bartenders, among them the Greenpoint and the Bensonhurst, and the Red Hook remains the most famous of the family.
tommys-margarita: Julio Bermejo created Tommy's Margarita in the early 1990s at Tommy's Mexican Restaurant in San Francisco, the family restaurant his parents had opened and named after his father, Tomás. Bermejo wanted the agave spirit to lead, so he left out the orange liqueur and balanced 100 percent agave tequila and lime with agave nectar, then an unusual ingredient behind the bar. The restaurant became known among bartenders for its tequila list, and the International Bartenders Association later added the recipe to its official list.
trinidad-sour: Giuseppe González created the Trinidad Sour in 2009 while bartending at the Clover Club in Brooklyn. He was inspired by the Trinidad Especial, a competition-winning drink by Italian bartender Valentino Bolognese that used Angostura bitters as its base with pisco and lime, and reworked the idea with rye, lemon and orgeat. The name nods to Trinidad, where Angostura has been made since the late 19th century, and the drink caught on slowly as other bartenders championed it.
white-negroni: British bartender Wayne Collins improvised the White Negroni in 2001 at Vinexpo, the wine fair in Bordeaux, when he wanted a Negroni and could not find Campari or sweet vermouth. He reached for French substitutes, the bitter gentian liqueur Suze and the aperitif wine Lillet Blanc, and mixed them with Plymouth gin. The pale result kept the Negroni's bitter structure in a new color and has become a standard variation. The original it imitates is credited to Count Camillo Negroni in Florence around 1919.
dirty-shirley: The Dirty Shirley is a Shirley Temple with vodka or rum added, and no one has claimed its invention; the non-alcoholic parent, named for the child film star, has been credited to Chasen's in West Hollywood, the Brown Derby and the Royal Hawaiian Hotel in Honolulu. The spiked version enjoyed a nostalgic revival in recent summers, when the New York Times asked whether it was the drink of the summer.
jello-shot: Satirist Tom Lehrer said he made the first modern Jell-O shots in the 1950s, mixing orange Jell-O with vodka to get around a ban on alcoholic drinks at a Christmas party on a naval base. Gelatin and spirits had met long before: Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide includes a punch jelly set with isinglass and spiked with cognac and rum. Jell-O shots faded in the 1960s and 1970s, then became common in American bars in the 1980s.
fish-house-punch: Fish House Punch is tied to the Schuylkill Fishing Company, a Philadelphia gentlemen's angling club founded in 1732 and later known as the State in Schuylkill, whose members gathered at their riverside fish house. The club's punch of rum, cognac and peach brandy with lemon and sugar is believed to date from its early years, and a Virginia visitor described being served a vast bowl of fine lemon punch there in 1744. The club still exists today.
sangria: Spaniards have mixed wine with fruit and spices since the Middle Ages, and the name sangria, from sangre, blood, for its deep red color, has been used for the drink since the 1700s. Spanish restaurants had reintroduced it to the United States as a chilled punch by the late 1940s, and it became widely known after the Spanish Pavilion served it at the 1964 New York World's Fair. Since 2014 EU labeling rules have reserved the plain name for sangria made in Spain and Portugal.
batanga: Don Javier Delgado Corona created the Batanga in 1961 at La Capilla, his cantina in the town of Tequila in Jalisco, mixing tequila, lime and cola over ice in a salt-rimmed glass and stirring each one with the long knife he used to cut limes. The name is usually said to come from a customer's nickname. Don Javier tended bar at La Capilla into his nineties and died in 2020, and the bar remains a destination for visitors to the town.
cantarito: The Cantarito comes from the tequila country of Jalisco, where it is sold at roadside stands and fairs, and no one has documented who first made it. Its name means little jug, after the unglazed clay cup it is served in, which keeps the mix of tequila, citrus juices, salt and grapefruit soda cool as moisture evaporates through the clay.
carajillo: The Carajillo is Spanish, though no one knows exactly where or when it began. One popular but unproven explanation says Spanish soldiers in colonial Cuba fortified their coffee with rum or brandy for courage, coraje, which became carajillo, while a Catalan story credits customers in Barcelona who ordered it with the words que ara guillo, I'm off now. In Mexico it took a new form, espresso shaken or poured over ice with Licor 43, the Spanish vanilla and citrus liqueur.
coquito: Coquito is a Puerto Rican Christmas tradition with no single inventor, usually seen as an island version of the eggnog-style holiday drinks of Europe, with coconut and Puerto Rican rum giving it a character of its own. Recipes are passed down in families, and the season runs from about Thanksgiving to Three Kings Day, when the Coquito Masters contest at El Museo del Barrio in New York celebrates it every year.
kalimotxo: Wine and cola had been mixed in the Basque Country before, but the Kalimotxo got its name in 1972 at the Puerto Viejo fiesta in Algorta, near Bilbao. As the story goes, friends running a drinks stall found their wine had turned and rescued it with Coca-Cola, and the name joins the nicknames of two of them, Kalimero and Motxongo. Simple and inexpensive, it spread through Basque fiestas and then across Spain.
michelada: The michelada has two origin stories. The more specific one credits Michel Ésper, a member of the Club Deportivo Potosino in San Luis Potosí, who in the 1960s asked for his beer with lime, salt and ice; other members began ordering Michel's lemonade, or Michel-ada. The other explanation is purely linguistic, reading the name as mi chela helada, my cold beer, in Mexican slang. Either way, the drink grew from a simple beer with lime and salt into a spicier, sauce-laden version that varies from region to region across Mexico.
queens-park-swizzle: The Queen's Park Swizzle was created in the 1920s at the Queen's Park Hotel in Port of Spain, Trinidad, a grand hotel facing the Queen's Park Savannah, when Prohibition was sending Americans to the Caribbean in search of a legal drink. The hotel's bar built it on demerara rum, mint and the Angostura bitters made on the island, swizzled with a stick traditionally cut from a Caribbean tree, Quararibea turbinata. Trader Vic singled it out for praise in his 1946 book, and the drink outlived the hotel, which closed in 1996.
sgroppino: The Sgroppino comes from Venice, where it has long been served between courses or at the end of a meal, though its precise origins are not recorded. The name comes from the Venetian verb sgropar, to untie a knot, a nod to its place after a rich meal, and the classic version is lemon sorbet whisked with prosecco, the sparkling wine of the surrounding Veneto.
terremoto: Terremoto means earthquake, and several old Santiago bars claim the drink, among them La Piojera and El Hoyo. The best-known story, told at El Hoyo, says German reporters covering the 1985 earthquake tried the mix of sweet pipeño wine and pineapple ice cream, and one remarked that this was the real earthquake; La Piojera tells its own version, and neither is confirmed. Pipeño itself is a young, rustic wine traditionally stored in barrels called pipas, which gave it its name.
ti-punch: Ti' Punch is short for petit punch, small punch, in the French and Creole of the French Caribbean, and it belongs to Martinique, Guadeloupe and their neighbors rather than to any single inventor. It is defined by rhum agricole, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice rather than molasses, a style that took hold on Martinique as falling sugar prices pushed planters toward rum in the late 19th century. Hosts traditionally set out rum, limes and cane syrup and let each guest mix their own.
appletini: The Appletini began as the Adam's Apple Martini at Lola's, a West Hollywood restaurant, in 1996. By the usual account, owner Loren Dunsworth was encouraged to add a signature Ketel One drink, and a bartender named Adam mixed the vodka with DeKuyper Sour Apple Pucker and a splash of sweet and sour mix, giving it his own name. Shortened to Appletini, it became an emblem of the martini-glass craze of the late 1990s and 2000s.
fuzzy-navel: The Fuzzy Navel arrived with DeKuyper Peachtree Schnapps, which National Distillers launched in 1984 as the first peach schnapps on the American market. Peach schnapps and orange juice became its signature serve, and the name is a double pun, fuzzy for the skin of the peach and navel for the orange. Bartending writer Ray Foley has said he came up with it at the company's request, while other accounts credit the brand's advertising agency with the name.
harvey-wallbanger: The Harvey Wallbanger was largely a marketing creation: in 1969 McKesson Imports, which brought Galliano into the United States, built a campaign led by marketing director George Bednar around a cartoon surfer named Harvey and a Screwdriver topped with the golden Italian liqueur. Bartending instructor Donato 'Duke' Antone is often credited with the recipe, but the popular story that he invented it in 1952 for a Californian surfer is considered implausible by historians. The ads made it one of the most famous drinks of the 1970s.
midori-sour: Midori, the bright green melon liqueur made by the Japanese company Suntory, was launched in the United States in 1978 with a party at Studio 54 in New York; its name is simply the Japanese word for green. The Midori Sour, the liqueur mixed with citrus or sour mix, became its signature drink without any one bartender being credited for it, and its color made it a fixture of nightclub bars in the decade that followed.
mudslide: The Wreck Bar at Rum Point on Grand Cayman claims the Mudslide, created in the 1970s. The story goes that a customer asked for a White Russian, and the bartender, with no cream on hand, reached for Baileys Irish Cream instead, which had reached the market only a few years earlier. The combination of vodka, coffee liqueur and Irish cream stuck, and the Wreck Bar still serves it as the house specialty. Frozen, blended versions later spread through American restaurants.
rusty-nail: The Rusty Nail got its name in the United States in the early 1960s, and New York's 21 Club is often linked with the drink; in 1963 Gina MacKinnon, who headed the Drambuie company, publicly endorsed the name. The pairing of Scotch and Drambuie was older, served as the B.I.F., after the British Industries Fair, in 1937 and under other names since. Drambuie itself is tied to a legend that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the recipe to the MacKinnon clan after the failed Jacobite rising of 1745.
b-52: The usual story credits Peter Fich, head bartender at the Banff Springs Hotel in Alberta in the 1970s, who named his new drinks after favorite bands, albums and songs; this one honored the B-52's rather than the bomber. A customer who owned restaurants in Alberta put it on his menus, which led some to place its birth at the Keg Steakhouse in Calgary in 1977. A rival claim credits a bartender at Maxwell's Plum in New York, and neither story is well documented.
baby-guinness: The Baby Guinness, a float of Irish cream over dark coffee liqueur, has no recorded inventor and takes its name from its look, a miniature pint of the Dublin stout, though it contains no Guinness at all.
buttery-nipple: The Buttery Nipple, a layered American shooter of butterscotch schnapps under Irish cream, has no documented inventor or date.
green-tea-shot: The Green Tea Shot, an American bar shooter of Irish whiskey, peach schnapps and sour mix, has no documented creator and contains no tea, taking its name from its pale green color.
jagerbomb: No one has documented who first dropped a shot of Jägermeister, the herbal liqueur from Wolfenbüttel in Germany, into a glass of energy drink to make the Jägerbomb.
kamikaze: The Kamikaze, an equal-parts mix of vodka, triple sec and lime, has no documented inventor or date, and its name is probably taken from the Japanese word, meaning divine wind, used for the suicide pilots of the Second World War.
lemon-drop-shot: The Lemon Drop was created in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday, owner of Henry Africa's in San Francisco's Russian Hill, widely described as America's first fern bar, the plant-filled style of bar that flourished in that decade. Named after the lemon drop candy, the vodka, lemon and sugar drink was first served up in a cocktail glass, and by the early 1990s bartenders were also pouring it as a shot.
mind-eraser: The Mind Eraser, a layered American highball of vodka and coffee liqueur topped with soda water, has no documented inventor or date.
pickleback: Bartender Reggie Cunningham is credited with the Pickleback, first poured in 2006 at the Bushwick Country Club, a bar in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, that kept a jar of pickles from McClure's, a local company. The story goes that a customer asked for a shot of the brine to follow her whiskey, and Cunningham tried the pairing and began serving it. By 2011 visitors had carried it to bars in London.
vegas-bomb: The Vegas Bomb, a shot of Canadian whisky, peach schnapps and cranberry juice dropped into an energy drink, has no documented inventor, though its name points to Las Vegas.
washington-apple: The Washington Apple, an American shooter of Canadian whisky, sour apple schnapps and cranberry juice, has no recorded inventor or date, and its name salutes Washington State, which grows most of the country's apples.
amaretto-sour: The Amaretto Sour was introduced in 1974 by the American importer of Amaretto di Saronno, the almond-flavored liqueur from Saronno near Milan, as a simple two-to-one mix of amaretto and lemon juice to sell the brand to American drinkers. It caught on, and through the 1980s most bars made it with premixed sour mix, which earned it a reputation as a sweet starter drink. In 2012 Portland bartender Jeffrey Morgenthaler published a rebuilt version with fresh lemon, egg white and a measure of cask-proof bourbon, and many bars now follow his approach.
aviation: Hugo Ensslin, head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York, created the Aviation and printed it in his 1916 book Recipes for Mixed Drinks: gin, lemon, maraschino and crème de violette. The name presumably reflects the excitement around flight in those years, and the violet liqueur gave the drink a sky-colored tint. When Harry Craddock included it in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book he left out the violette, and as the liqueur vanished from American shelves, generations of bartenders followed his colorless version until crème de violette returned to the market in 2007.
bees-knees: The Bee's Knees belongs to the Prohibition years of the 1920s, and its name is the era's slang for something excellent. Its inventor is uncertain: a 1929 newspaper item credited Margaret Brown, the Titanic survivor remembered as the Unsinkable Molly Brown, while others point to Frank Meier, who ran the bar at the Ritz in Paris from 1921. Honey and lemon are often said to have masked the harsh taste of bathtub gin, a plausible explanation that nobody has proved.
blood-and-sand: Blood and Sand takes its name from the 1922 film in which Rudolph Valentino played a doomed matador, and the red cherry liqueur and orange juice are often read as a nod to the bullring. Its creator is unknown, but the recipe was preserved in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy hotel in London, and after decades of obscurity craft bartenders revived it.
brandy-crusta: Joseph Santini created the Brandy Crusta in the 1850s at his New Orleans bar, the Jewel of the South. The name comes from the crust of sugar around the rim of the glass, set off by a long spiral of lemon peel lining the inside. Jerry Thomas published it in his landmark 1862 bar guide, giving it national reach. Its mix of brandy, orange curaçao and lemon is widely seen as the ancestor of the Sidecar, and a New Orleans bar that took the name Jewel of the South revived both the name and the drink in 2019.
caipirinha: The Caipirinha grew up in the interior of São Paulo state. One popular account dates it to around 1918, when a folk remedy of lime, garlic and honey circulating during the Spanish flu was mixed with cachaça, and over time the garlic and honey gave way to sugar and ice. Others trace it to 19th-century landowners in the Piracicaba sugarcane region, who served it at gatherings. The name is a diminutive of caipira, a term for country people from rural São Paulo, and Brazilian law now defines the drink as cachaça with lime and sugar.
clover-club: The Clover Club cocktail takes its name from the Clover Club, a Philadelphia gathering of lawyers, writers and businessmen founded in 1882 that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel. Recipes for its mix of gin, lemon, raspberry and egg white appeared in print from around 1908, and it spread to the smart bars of New York before fading after Prohibition; a 1939 drink book dismissed it outright. Revived in the craft era, it lent its name to Julie Reiner's Clover Club bar in Brooklyn, opened in 2008.
corpse-reviver-no-2: Corpse revivers were a loose 19th-century family of pick-me-up drinks, but the No. 2 is fixed in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy hotel in London: equal parts gin, Cointreau, Kina Lillet and lemon juice with a dash of absinthe. The drink fell from view for decades until craft bartenders revived it in the early 2000s, and it is now the best-known of its family.
cosmopolitan: Several bartenders claim the Cosmopolitan: Neal Murray said he created it in 1975 at the Cork & Cleaver in Minneapolis by adding cranberry to a Kamikaze, John Caine is credited with popularizing a version in San Francisco, and historian Gary Regan credited Cheryl Cook in South Beach, Miami, in the mid-1980s. The version most bars use was refined in the late 1980s by Toby Cecchini at the Odeon in New York, with Absolut Citron, Cointreau, cranberry and fresh lime. Madonna and then Carrie Bradshaw of Sex and the City made it a global icon.
daiquiri: The daiquiri is named for Daiquirí, a beach and mining village near Santiago de Cuba, where American mining engineer Jennings Cox is credited with mixing rum, lime and sugar around 1898. Those ingredients were already familiar in Cuba, but the name stuck to Cox's version. US Navy officer Lucius Johnson brought it to the Army and Navy Club in Washington in 1909, and in Havana, Constantino Ribalaigua of El Floridita refined it in the 1920s and 1930s, creating the frozen variations Ernest Hemingway favored.
